sections.title: Intuition is for everyone, so why is this page created specifically for athletes?

blocks.body: Because I believe that intuition is essential in sport.

Throughout their careers, athletes often experience a powerful connection to their intuition. At least once, every competitive athlete has experienced moments when they instinctively know something that goes beyond the logical next step, their coach’s instructions or an agreed strategy.

blocks.text: The momentum, instinct, feel for the game — whatever you call it.

blocks.body:
They bring an immediate sense of flow and clarity — an inner shift that changes the outer reality. 

How long and deep this connection goes often determines an athlete’s ability to turn a difficult situation in their favour, stay present and creative, and enjoy their performance.

blocks.text:
The only person you’re ever competing against is yourself. The rest is out of your control.
— John Wooden, basketball coach.

blocks.alt: Close-up portrait: part of a woman’s face, looking at the camera

blocks.text:
"Faith is rewarded, perhaps, even more than talent or ability. ... We are required to believe in something that doesn't exist in order to allow it to come into being." 
— Rick Rubin, record producer

blocks.body: A space to develop the ability to connect with yourself, listen to your inner voice and recognise what it is saying.

blocks.heading: Intuition speaks differently to everyone
blocks.body: For some, intuition comes as a gut feeling or a sensation in the heart; for others, as a voice, an image, a sudden flash of insight, or even something that appears in a dream. Sometimes it arrives instantly and clearly; at other times it is subtle and needs silence, patience and attention to notice.

blocks.heading: Where we begin
blocks.body: Our work begins with exploring what intuition means to you: how you naturally perceive it, how it shows up in different situations, and what helps you recognise its signals. You learn to notice, distinguish and interpret these messages, while developing the confidence to trust your own perceptions.

blocks.text: As with any new experience, curiosity, courage, openness and trust are essential. Above all, a willingness to explore, to experience something new, yet familiar.

blocks.heading: Inner alignment and trust
blocks.body: Intuition can reconnect us with our inner truth: our values, what makes us happy, what we want from life and how we wish to move through it. Yet this journey is not only about understanding and answers. It is also about learning to accept the unknown, the unpredictable and the uncontrollable. Letting go of the boundaries that stand in the way of your inner alignment and contentment is one of the few skills we practise.

blocks.text: When we're doing what we love, we don't have to justify it to ourselves or others.  Not everything in life can be understood through logic, nor does everything need to be.

blocks.heading: How the sessions work
blocks.body:
These sessions are led intuitively and individually. There is no predefined programme designed for everyone. My approach is not based on scientific studies or established concepts, but neither does it seek to deny or exclude any particular perspective.

It is not psychological counselling or conventional mental training, though we may touch on some elements of those methods. Sessions normally unfold naturally, instinctively: your intuition will lead us to where your attention and awareness are most needed.

blocks.title: What we can explore together
blocks.intro: Connecting to intuition on a deeper level can help athletes navigate both sport and life with greater awareness, balance and self-trust. These are a few examples of what we might explore.
blocks.d1: Staying connected to the process rather than fixating on the result.
blocks.d2: Telling it apart from fears, mental chatter and external expectations.
blocks.d3: Building a deeper relationship with it, and learning to notice what it is telling you.
blocks.d4: Accepting periods of uncertainty, crisis, rest, growth and change as natural parts of everyone’s path.
blocks.d5: Expressing yourself beyond social pressure and rigid ideas of what is right or wrong, possible or impossible.
blocks.d6: Shifting attention and energy towards other meaningful aspects of life, and developing an identity beyond sport.
blocks.finalText: Checking with yourself before and after listening to the advice of family, friends, coaches, doctors and other experts. No one knows whats right for you better than you.

blocks.text:
"Become who you are."
— Fredrick Nietzsche, philosopher

blocks.heading: Step back from expectations
blocks.body:
Sometimes, no matter how much we want to, we struggle to hear or recognise the voice of our intuition.

To build a reality of our own, we need to be authentic. We need to find strength in who we truly are, rather than in who we were taught or expected to be. We need to learn to respect everything we feel — even, and especially, when we believe there is something profoundly wrong with us.

blocks.text: After years of parental advice, education and social conditioning, in our attempt to fit in, we often drift far away from who we truly are.

blocks.body: When this gap becomes too big to ignore, we may begin to recognise it through a persistent sense of inner confusion, constant pressure or, in more extreme cases, a void where nothing feels alive or purposeful. Things that once mattered lose their power. What used to bring us joy, purpose and satisfaction no longer has the same effect.

blocks.heading: Rediscovering what feels like you
blocks.body: Initially, we tend to dismiss these shifts, calling them moods or temporary phases. We tell ourselves that once we achieve our next goal, we'll finally be happy.

blocks.text: Eventually, we realise that no people, no amount of money and no number of medals can fill the void within us. It can only be filled with love, self love.

blocks.body:
More often than not, a change in our outer circumstances brings only momentary relief. An achievement brings a moment of ecstasy, only to be followed by the setting of an even bigger goal when the previous one fails to deliver the fulfilment we expected.

Perhaps this is an invitation to step back, reflect and rediscover — or perhaps recall — what makes us unique, fulfilled and whole.

blocks.heading: Unplug
blocks.body: At this stage, social pressure can be particularly strong. People may offer well-meaning advice, but the real journey is a private and inward one. Stepping onto this path can bring a temporary sense of social alienation, and that's normal. At this point, building a relationship with yourself becomes so much more important.

blocks.text: You may feel disconnected from everything familiar without yet having a clear sense of what comes next. That uncertainty deserves to be acknowledged and accepted rather than immediately fixed.

blocks.heading: How I can support here
blocks.body:
What I offer is simply to be a witness — a steady presence as you navigate these shifts, to normalise and name what you’re experiencing. Find the comfort to relax in the unknown, even when it feels uncomfortable.

This is deep and individual work, but everyone sometimes needs a hand to hold in these moments. Of course, it’s not a hand you rely on forever. Much of the journey you walk alone, but a witness — someone who can name your experience as valid and normal — can make the difference.

I speak from my own journey, and what I offer is to be that hand, that witness, friend and perhaps even that guide, whenever you need it.

blocks.text: Although I am not an athlete myself, sport has always been part of my life.

blocks.body:
From joining grassroots sports clubs as a child to becoming a passionate sports fan and eventually working as a Competition Manager at one of the world’s largest sports organisations, my journey has taken me through many different sides of sport.

During my ten years at FIFA, I contributed to the organisation of football World Cups, as well as numerous related events. Along the way, I met athletes at different stages of their careers, each with their own backgrounds, experiences, ambitions, and challenges. Through these encounters, I gradually developed a deeper interest in the person behind the athlete — their individual journey, their inner world, and the challenges that may remain unseen from the outside. Over time, I began to envision a space where athletes could find support beyond their sporting achievements.

A few years ago, my own life took a turn that had been brewing within me for some time. I left a successful career without knowing what would come next. This gave me space to pause and look inward, to reflect on who I really am and what I want. I delved into psychology, body and energy practices, alternative medicine and healing approaches,  ancient philosophies. I explored my own perceptions and senses, experimented, and gradually discovered new ways of understanding myself and the world around me. Most importantly, I started feeling gratitude for this life and with less having more. 

I've always been intuitive, since I remember myself. Unfortunately, my sensitivity was often dismissed and not taken seriously by my family, so I never learned to trust it. Over the past few years, however, I have managed to find my own voice beneath layers of family conditioning and social expectations. I have learned to trust myself more deeply and rely less on external validation or the need for constant control and security. This journey continues to this day.

blocks.text: Today, through the individual sessions I offer, I am bringing this idea of creating a supportive space for athletes to life. Guiding others in their search for self-trust, fulfilment, and happiness has become a meaningful part of my own journey.
